Beyond submitting a proposed commission structure for purchases made through the App Store IAP system within the United States, Apple also filed a motion expressing willingness to explore a settlement with Epic Games. Below are the relevant details.

Apple may be ready to settle

Apple submitted a proposal this morning outlining the commissions it hopes to be permitted to charge for purchases completed through payment systems outside the App Store.

The timing of this filing coincides with the Supreme Court responding to Apple's request to stay the lower court proceedings while it reviews Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers's contempt ruling. Apple was found in contempt after it chose to charge a 27% commission despite being ordered by the court to allow developers to direct users to external payment methods.

Under Apple's proposed structure, it could charge up to a 15% commission on purchases completed through alternative payment systems. Epic Games immediately objected, stating that it "believes these fees are well outside the range contemplated by the Ninth Circuit's guidance on permissible fee levels."

Although that document attracted much attention, Apple also filed another motion today asking Judge Gonzalez Rogers to order both parties into a settlement conference.

Filing contents (edited for clarity):

This suggests that Apple's legal team had already reached out to Epic's lawyers to discuss requesting a settlement conference before filing the motion, but Epic did not agree to Apple's request.

In the filing, Apple argues that the court has the authority to order both parties into a settlement conference without Epic's consent, and adds that the Ninth Circuit itself has also encouraged both parties to reach agreement on an appropriate "outbound" commission.

The company also stated that "discussing potential settlement options in a confidential, non-adversarial environment will increase the likelihood of reaching a pragmatic resolution, thereby avoiding a lengthy remand process."

Worth noting is that this filing does not contain any specific terms or offers from Apple regarding a settlement, nor does it constitute a genuine settlement proposal. Apple is only requesting that the court order both parties to conduct settlement negotiations under the supervision of Magistrate Judge Joseph C. Spero.
